scope_note: KTM/Husqvarna/GasGas MX and cross-country models. Findings are paraphrased from the article text that WebFetch returned. Video-only pages are listed as builds with parts and no observations. Part numbers appear only where the source gave them; most sources gave none.

feedback.product: XACT PRO 7548 cone-valve coil fork (5.0 N/mm) + XACT PRO 8950 shock (45 N/mm), as fitted to 2026-1/2 Factory Edition
feedback.author: Ron Lawson
feedback.conditions: Glen Helen. The article compares the FE against the standard 450 SX-F, which has the WP AER fork and XACT LDS shock.
feedback.observed: Fork: a major improvement aimed at expert riders. Heavier or less experienced riders may want to soften it, and backing off rebound adds comfort. Shock: a step up over standard but not dramatic; the main gain is the worm-gear preload adjuster. The author thinks suspension was the only thing that held the KTM back in past shootouts. The Akrapovic slip-on made little performance difference but is somewhat quieter.
feedback.other_mods: Factory Edition kit: Akrapovic slip-on, Hinson clutch cover (KTM clutch internals), semi-floating front disc, CUO, CNC clamps, holeshot device. MSRP $13,699.

feedback.product: Stage 1 head work (hand-ported, decked, new intake guides, recut seats), stiffer valve springs, new air boot, second injector, Vortex ECU map
feedback.author: Josh Mosiman
feedback.conditions: Ezra Lewis raced it at the AMA Hangtown National and crashed in the LCQ. Mosiman rode it at Cahuilla, Glen Helen and Mammoth (about 8,000 ft); a Saturday crash meant he did not race.
feedback.observed: Pulled hard and power-wheelied easily; Ezra called it fast enough to be a little alarming but did not tire quickly on it. Both riders said it sounded like a factory 250. Ran on ETS MX18 fuel.
feedback.measured: No dyno figures. Package price $5,066.09 for parts and labor, fuel not included.
feedback.other_mods: REP-revalved WP XACT Pro fork and shock, Fasst Flexx bars, Guts seat, 53T rear sprocket (stock 51T), Dunlop MX34

feedback.product: Revalve of stock WP XACT Pro fork and shock (titanium shims, new spring retainers, hidden shock bladder, new shock spring)
feedback.author: Josh Mosiman
feedback.conditions: Pro and expert riders at Hangtown, Cahuilla, Glen Helen and Mammoth. The team kept the stock air fork instead of A-kit cone-valve forks.
feedback.observed: Ezra liked the stiffer setting. MXA says a correctly set up WP air fork now feels more like a spring fork. Mosiman found it firm for his riding but appreciated it on the rough Mammoth track.
feedback.measured: Price $1,092.82; typical range $900-$1,400.

feedback.product: Flexx handlebar (hard red rebound dampers, yellow medium compression dampers)
feedback.author: Josh Mosiman
feedback.conditions: Mosiman's personal setup on the MXA race build
feedback.observed: More hand comfort without vagueness at turn-in. No negatives stated.

feedback.product: 53T rear sprocket (from stock 51T)
feedback.author: Josh Mosiman
feedback.conditions: Mammoth, about 8,000 ft altitude
feedback.observed: Helped pulling power at altitude, but the bike ran through the gears quickly.

feedback.product: Full Performance linkage (KTM/GasGas)

bike.model: SX-F (2024.5-2025.5 KTM/GasGas platform; specific test bike not confirmed)

feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Several MXA test riders. A shock spring one rate stiffer is required. Ride recommends 106-108mm race sag; MXA normally runs 105mm. Fits 2024.5, 2025 and 2025.5 KTM/GasGas, plus 2025 Husqvarna (raises standard Husky rear to KTM height). Does not fit 2023-2024 because the linkage bolts changed.
feedback.observed: Better stability on corner entry and long fast straights. The stiffer spring stopped the shock sitting low under hard acceleration, which improved traction. Riders could run softer fork clickers because the shock loaded the fork less, and the bike was more consistent lap to lap. MXA says it fixes a tall-feeling, unbalanced rear. Before the swap, smaller riders had said the shock sat too high on corner entry; lowering the rear and opening damping helped but made it harsh on acceleration bumps. Downsides: the spring is mandatory and adds cost; no 2023-2024 fitment.
feedback.measured: Linkage $474.90; about $600 with the spring; about 20 minutes to install.

feedback.product: KTM/Husqvarna/GasGas 250F second injector kit (in OEM KTM air boot) + XPR-tuned Vortex ECU

bike.model: 250F (the article says 'GasGas FC250'; probably the MC 250F)

feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Stock engine plus the kit and an XPR Vortex map; MXA test riders
feedback.observed: Faster throttle pickup; reaches the powerband without relying on revs or the clutch. Better midrange and over-rev, so it felt like a modified engine. The rear wheel felt more connected. Durability should match stock because there is no internal work. Downsides: fuel-line routing is hard (MXA advises professional install), the stock ECU won't run it, and the total cost is about $2,000.
feedback.measured: No dyno. $945 for the kit; $2,004 with a tuned Vortex; $400 to remap a non-XPR Vortex.

feedback.product: Slip-on muffler (KTM PowerParts)
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA race test of the FE
feedback.observed: Durable with smooth power. It mates only to the stock head pipe because the Akrapovic head pipe has a different diameter, so going further means buying the full Akrapovic system.
feedback.measured: Price just under $900

feedback.product: WP split triple clamps
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA race test
feedback.observed: Testers kept the stock geometry and did not consider the clamps a performance upgrade, though they look good. This disagrees with Keefer's positive findings on aftermarket 23.5mm offset clamps (ktm-fb-013).

feedback.product: Factory wheelset
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA race test
feedback.observed: Stronger than stock, but the spokes still loosen during break-in; MXA tightens them after every moto and recommends a Fasst Company spoke torque wrench. MXA also notes that WP 6500 or KYB spring-fork conversions make a bike ineligible for AMA Amateur stock classes.
feedback.measured: Over $1,000

feedback.brand: KTM PowerParts / Nihilo Concepts / Ride Engineering / Twin Air
feedback.product: Connectivity Unit Offroad (CUO) retrofit; start/stop button relocation (Nihilo, Ride Engineering); radiator cap tool (Nihilo); Twin Air airbox wash covers
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA race test of the stock bike
feedback.observed: Fixes for stock annoyances: the kill button is on the right bar (relocation buttons move it left), the plastic radiator cap is hard to remove (tool), and the airbox vents let water in when washing (Twin Air covers). The CUO adds maps, traction control, launch control and data logging. Some testers remove the stock frame guards because their thickness pushes the feet out. MXA suggests a DIY hole of about 1-1/4 inch in the right side panel to reach the shock clickers.
feedback.measured: CUO $249.99; LitPro $69.99 per year

feedback.product: Slip-on muffler
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA race test
feedback.observed: Cited as a source of added performance together with CUO map settings; no detail given. The same test liked the FE's Brembo brakes (in place of BrakTec) and the WP holeshot device, and credited the ribbed Guts seat cover with stopping the rider sliding back under acceleration.

feedback.product: 23.5mm offset split triple clamps
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Baseline-and-mods article for riders around 175-200 lb. Keefer has not tested other split-clamp brands.
feedback.observed: Calmer off-throttle, more front-end feel, less firm over braking bumps, and turns into ruts better.
feedback.other_mods: FMF exhaust, Vortex ECU (XPR), WP XACT Pro 6500 fork

feedback.product: Full system for 2023+ KTM 450 SX-F (model not named in the summary; insert kept in)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Insert kept in on the 450 (removed on the 350). Keefer has not tried every available muffler.
feedback.observed: More midrange and top-end pull and better torque feel out of corners, with slightly less low end and slightly less rpm response.

feedback.product: Vortex ECU with XPR map
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: The stock ECU is locked on newer KTMs, so a replacement unit is needed. Keefer also tried the AIM Taipan and rated it below the Vortex because fewer tuners know it and it is harder to get.
feedback.observed: More usable second gear in corners, more linear low end, more mid-to-top pull, and better rear traction.

feedback.product: XACT Pro 6500 cartridge kit (closed-cartridge coil conversion for 48mm AER fork; 'comfort' or 'performance' setting)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Riders around 175-200 lb. Keefer used REP/AEO settings and worked with REP on comfort settings for the 2023 chassis.
feedback.observed: The stock setting gives more front-end feel and initial-lean traction than the AER fork, but damping feels off near the end of the stroke. The comfort setting has some mid-stroke harshness, and the performance setting can be harsh at the edge of the tire.
feedback.measured: Price about $1,400 as stated. Stock AER baseline for comparison: 10.9 bar, 5mm fork height, C 14 out, R 15 out; shock sag 103mm, LSC 12 out, HSC 1.25 out, R 15 out.

feedback.product: Pro Taper Husqvarna Stock EVO bend cut to 800-803mm; alternative FASST Co. FLEXX 12-degree Moto
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Baseline-and-mods article
feedback.observed: The Pro Taper EVO cuts vibration and is more comfortable on the hands. The Flexx gives the most flex but takes time to get used to visually.
feedback.measured: Pro Taper cut width 800-803mm

feedback.product: XACT Pro 6500 cartridge fork kit (drop-in AER-to-coil), valved by AEO Powersports

bike.model: XACT AER-equipped models (test bike not stated)

feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Several MXA test riders on several tracks; AEO valving; 5.3 N/mm springs. HSC on the shock went a quarter turn stiffer to rebalance.
feedback.observed: Better small-bump comfort and ground tracking, no late-stroke ramp-up, planted feel, and consistent across tracks with no air-pressure changes. Extra rebound helped riders with slower turn-entry speeds. Downsides: the added weight makes the front feel slow and heavy when changing lines and it wiggles off-throttle. It also changed rear balance, so the rear hopped off-throttle until HSC was adjusted. Expensive. MXA verdict: 'drop-in plushness'. Compare with Keefer (ktm-fb-016), who found end-stroke damping off and some setting-dependent harshness.
feedback.measured: Adds 3.5 lb over the AER fork. Kit $1,299; springs $135; about $1,500 installed with oil, bushings and valving.

feedback.product: Factory 4.1 RCT titanium/carbon (mid-pipe/muffler combo plus titanium head pipe)
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA testers; loamy corners mentioned. Fits 2023 450 XC-F, 2023.5 450 SX-F FE, 2023 FC450/FX450/Rockstar and 2023.5 MC450F FE.
feedback.observed: Snappier throttle response, especially in loam, more low end, and easier to carry third gear through tight corners. Pulling the insert adds midrange, but testers preferred it in for friendlier delivery. Top end close to stock with the insert in. No complaints. The stainless version is said to perform the same for less.
feedback.measured: No stock-vs-FMF dyno comparison. The article claims close to 60 hp; torque is given as 36.31 lb-ft in the meta description and 37.01 lb-ft in the body, which is inconsistent. Prices: $799.99 combo, $449.99 head pipe, $1,249.99 complete.

feedback.product: Factory Fatty pipe + Titanium Powercore 2.1 silencer
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Dyno plus track by MXA testers, green map
feedback.observed: More snap and bottom-end hit than the dyno suggests, with cleaner throttle response. Easier to hold third gear in corners. Slight loss between 5800 and 6700 rpm, then gains up top. No complaints.
feedback.measured: Stock: 54.96 hp @ 8560 rpm, 35.38 lb-ft @ 7450 rpm. FMF: 58.08 hp @ 8800 rpm, 36.10 lb-ft @ 7750 rpm (green map). Prices: Fatty $299.99, Powercore 2.1 $229.99, Ti Powercore 2.1 $449.99.

feedback.product: Factory Fatty pipe + Titanium Powercore 2.1 silencer (and Powercore 2.1 alone on stock pipe)
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Dyno plus track, green map
feedback.observed: Smoother curve without the stock dip between 7600 and 8000 rpm; can be ridden a gear higher. The silencer alone adds mid and top power, which suits dry, slick tracks, but has less bottom snap than the full system.
feedback.measured: Stock: 52.12 hp @ 8600 rpm, 32.17 lb-ft @ 8150 rpm. FMF: 53.38 hp @ 8800 rpm, 32.40 lb-ft @ 8250 rpm (green map).

feedback.product: Pro Circuit pipe (stock silencer) + Twisted Development ECU remap
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: MXA race test. The 2023-24 Continental ECUs are locked and Vortex units are incompatible; WMR and Jamie Ellis cracked the stock ECU.
feedback.observed: Can use third gear in the tightest corners and revs further. The remap keeps the lugging bottom end, adds throttle response and mid-to-top pull, and cuts rev-limiter hits. MXA said the combination 'brought our 2024 KTM 300SX to life.'

feedback.product: National rear shock for 2025+ KTM/Husqvarna/GasGas 85 platform
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: 12-year-old intermediate rider; MX-Tech set it up for his height, weight and skill
feedback.observed: More planted and stable than the stock WP XACT on acceleration bumps, landings and choppy corners. Absorbs square edges and braking bumps, so less fatigue. Resists bottoming with progressive rather than harsh damping. Clickers are noticeable, unlike stock. Downsides: high price, and the extra mid-speed adjuster can complicate setup for parents.

feedback.product: Vortex ECU mapping + TD exhaust flange
feedback.author: Eddie Laret (as given in the fetched summary)
feedback.conditions: 6'1", 220 lb rider; compared after a few days on the stock bike
feedback.observed: More low-end torque and drive out of soft corners, better third-gear roll-on, and more response from bottom to mid while keeping the linear feel.
feedback.other_mods: Technical Touch KYB conversion, X-Trig ROCS clamps, Moto-Master 270mm brake

feedback.product: KYB spring fork conversion kit (SSS inner chamber, springs, billet fork lugs), valved by Shock Therapy
feedback.author: Eddie Laret (as given in the fetched summary)
feedback.conditions: 220 lb rider; Glen Helen; fork and shock valved for the rider
feedback.observed: Less harsh than the AER48, more consistent over long motos, less edgy at Glen Helen, and less rigid on square-edged hardpack while staying plush on slap-downs.

feedback.product: ROCS triple clamps with PHDS bar mounts (stock 22mm offset)
feedback.author: Eddie Laret (as given in the fetched summary)
feedback.conditions: Stock 22mm offset
feedback.observed: The PHDS bushings cut hand vibration, though frame vibration remains. Slightly better front-end feel and corner traction, with a more positive front tire on entry.

feedback.product: Factory Billet front caliper + 270mm oversize front rotor
feedback.author: Eddie Laret (as given in the fetched summary)
feedback.conditions: Compared with the stock Brembo
feedback.observed: Softer, more linear lever feel under heavy braking and less grabby when dragging the brake through ruts, which keeps the chassis calmer. Helps prevent front washouts when entering corners hot; laps were more consistent.

feedback.product: Engine mount kit (billet upper mounts, titanium front mount bolt, split right-side mount)
feedback.author: Donn Maeda
feedback.conditions: Varied dirt. The fork had an Enzo KYB spring conversion and the shock was revalved.
feedback.observed: More comfort in braking bumps, more front grip and confidence on turn-in, more precise at the apex, more predictable sliding under power, and settles faster on slap-downs. Expensive.
feedback.other_mods: Enzo Racing KYB spring conversion, revalved shock

feedback.product: Factory 4.1 titanium full system
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Keefer's personal race bike; local race at Glen Helen (rough, ruts, braking bumps, slick sections)
feedback.observed: More mid-rpm response and midrange pull, more top end, and over-rev equal to stock. Packing needs service every 10-12 engine hours; a blowout can damage the titanium can.
feedback.measured: 'Almost two pounds' lighter than stock
feedback.other_mods: REP suspension and linkage, XPR Vortex, ZRT throttle, Pro Taper EVO bars, ETS MX18

feedback.product: CV fork setting + Trax shock + linkage
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Glen Helen race
feedback.observed: More comfort over small and braking bumps, better front traction in shallow ruts, better rear hold-up, and less sitting low under throttle. Keefer calls it the most comfortable WP Pro Components setup he has run. The linkage ratio needs a shock spring change, the front feels low under heavy braking (he may go stiffer), and earlier CV settings were harsher.

feedback.product: Vortex ECU mapped for FMF 4.1 and ETS MX18
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Glen Helen race
feedback.observed: More low-end torque, response, midrange and over-rev; runs clean with no popping; better throttle feel on slick sections. Keefer's first engine mod. ETS MX18 had to be mapped by a tuner.
feedback.measured: Cost '1000.00 or so'

feedback.product: Throttle tube (milled down by ZRT)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Glen Helen race
feedback.observed: Smaller feel in the hand, smoother roll and lighter pull, so less right-arm fatigue. In a 2021 article Keefer adds that it needs setup (cutting the right side of the bar) and is expensive.

feedback.product: KYB spring fork conversion kit + Enzo-revalved WP shock
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: About 15 hours on the bike; 230 lb rider. A revalved AER was tried first and never felt comfortable. Ride height went to full length instead of Husky's 10mm-lower setting, using the KTM 2023 linkage on KTM's advice (the stock Husky linkage risked the tire contacting the fender).
feedback.observed: Better front grip on lean, plusher on slap-downs and bumps, and less mid-corner washing. Final tweaks were one click slower rebound and a stiffer fork spring. The revalved shock gave better support for the heavy rider and more low-speed damping on acceleration.
feedback.other_mods: Vortex/TD map, FMF 4.1 slip-on, ZRT throttle, Pro Taper Fuzion 996, Works Connection axle blocks and Pro Launch

feedback.product: Vortex ECU with TD mapping
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: 230 lb rider
feedback.observed: The stock map felt slightly lean at parts of the throttle and popped on decel. The TD map gave more power everywhere, better rear-wheel connection and traction, and smoother response in soft dirt.

feedback.product: Factory 4.1 slip-on vs 4.1 full system
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Subjective comparison against stock; no track given
feedback.observed: Slip-on: more low-to-mid response, midrange pull, top end and over-rev, but less bottom-end pull than stock. Insert in gives better rear-wheel connection; out gives more rpm feel. Full system: more midrange once out of the corner and more top/over-rev, but some low-rpm response lost. Both need packing every 10-12 hours. In the 'top five mods' article on the same bike, Keefer instead reports the slip-on gave stronger bottom-end pull (ktm-fb-033), so his two articles conflict on bottom end.
feedback.measured: Slip-on nearly 2 lb lighter than stock; full system about 1 lb lighter (as stated).

feedback.product: Pro Launch device (set at 130mm) and Elite axle blocks
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Tall, heavy rider (230 lb)
feedback.observed: The launch device keeps the front down off the start and is easy to install and reliable. The axle blocks make chain adjustment easier but gave no noticeable rear traction gain. That disagrees with Keefer's 2020-2022 KTM/Husky articles, where floating axle blocks freed the rear on acceleration chop (ktm-fb-041).
feedback.measured: Launch setting 130mm

feedback.product: TD exhaust flange
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: No remap needed; installs in minutes
feedback.observed: Better response from mid-corner to exit, more exit pull and better third-gear lugging. Revs pick up quicker, so the bike feels lighter on bumpy tracks.

feedback.product: 14/52 gearing (stock 13/49); 48 N/m shock spring for riders 195 lb+; swingarm pivot 95 Nm
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Fast, choppy tracks such as Glen Helen; 195 lb tester for the spring
feedback.observed: 14/52 gives more midrange recovery and a freer shock on acceleration but needs a new chain. 95 Nm on the pivot gives a more planted feel and rear traction, but may flex too much on deep-tilled tracks.
feedback.measured: Engine hangers 28 Nm; pivot 95 Nm instead of 100 Nm

feedback.product: Race Team bend (W810 H91 R49 S52)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Riders about 5'8" to 6'1"
feedback.observed: The stock bar is low and flat. The Race Team bend adds standing height, which helps the rider get over the front. Alternatively, cut the stock bar to 805mm to help cornering.

feedback.product: KTM 250 SX two-stroke air filter cage (no backfire screen)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Several months of riding
feedback.observed: Better low-to-mid throttle response; the cheapest and easiest mod.

feedback.product: Works Connection Elite axle blocks or Ride Engineering axle/block kit (removes fixed left block)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Repeated across the 2020 KTM 450, 2021 KTM 250/350 and 2022 FC450 articles
feedback.observed: The rear moves more freely under throttle and is more comfortable over acceleration chop. In the 2023 FC350 article Keefer found no noticeable traction gain (ktm-fb-036).

feedback.product: Pro Taper SX Race bend (800W, 87H, 54.5 rise, 54 sweep); Ride Engineering one-piece oversize bar mount
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Riders 5'8" to 6'1"
feedback.observed: The Pro Taper bar is more comfortable than the stiff stock Neken and gives a better standing feel. The Ride Engineering mount resists the twisting and bending of the stock mount in corner crashes.

feedback.product: Honda CRF450R rubber-covered brake pedal spring; Fasst Co rear brake return spring
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Durability observation
feedback.observed: The stock KTM spring vibrates and breaks every 4-5 hours (3-4 hours in the 2020 article). The Honda spring avoids that. The Fasst spring works in compression, giving tunable pedal resistance and a less on-off feel.

feedback.product: Vortex ECU (TD Racing map)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Track riding
feedback.observed: Smoother delivery, more rear-wheel connection and less spin, more power everywhere, and a longer pull in each gear. Keefer's single engine mod of choice. Downside: price.

feedback.product: 2019.5 Factory Edition triple clamps
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Back to back against the stock clamps, with the stock AER fork
feedback.observed: Softer initial feel on slap-downs, smoother over decel bumps, more comfort through the stroke, and better front grip in choppy ruts. Fork compression went slightly stiffer.

feedback.product: Factory 4.1 titanium full system
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Track riding
feedback.observed: Better low-to-mid response and midrange pull, more top end, and over-rev equal to stock. Packing every 10-12 hours. This verdict is repeated almost word for word in the 2021 KTM 250/350 and 2022 FC450 articles.
feedback.measured: About 2 lb lighter than stock; spring forks add about 3 lb back (as stated)

feedback.product: WP/KYB fork conversion kit (KYB AOS internals in WP tubes)
feedback.author: Kris Keefer
feedback.conditions: Bonus item in the 2020 KTM 450 SX-F mods article, ridden on the FC450; damping and springs set to the rider
feedback.observed: Better small-bump comfort and front feel than the AER, more control in rough sections, and less mid-stroke harshness late in the day. Still less comfortable over decel bumps than a Yamaha SSS fork.

feedback.product: Aero/Hybrid spring conversion kit (modified Ohlins TTX22 cartridge and coil spring in the damping leg; WP air leg kept)
feedback.author: Jody Weisel
feedback.conditions: Vets and slower riders: 4.5 N/mm spring, 14 clicks out compression and rebound, 55 psi in the air leg. Fast intermediates and pros: 4.7 N/mm if pressure would exceed 95 psi.
feedback.observed: Coil feel at the start of the stroke with an air ramp for bottoming. The Ohlins clickers are very effective (one click felt like about two on other forks), and air pressure tunes overall stiffness. Lighter than typical conversions. No complaints.
feedback.measured: $995 installed with spring and oil

feedback.product: Gen2 split triple clamps (stock 22mm offset) with optional Luxon bar mounts
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Track testing on braking bumps and corner entry
feedback.observed: More comfortable in braking bumps (similar to GasGas clamps) without losing the corner precision of the KTM clamps. The front end performed better overall, and the bar mounts resist twisting in tip-overs. Downsides: the KTM version has a machined Honda steering-damper mount that requires trimming the front fender if no damper is fitted, and the bar mounts add significant cost.
feedback.measured: Article says 18 g lighter than stock but elsewhere says the same weight (inconsistent). Torque: Luxon 12 Nm top / 8 Nm bottom vs KTM 20 / 15 (the article writes 'N/mm'). Prices $799.95 clamps; $989.95 with mounts.

feedback.product: Billet inner hub/pressure plate (+ clutch pack with stiffer Belleville, clutch cover)
feedback.author: MXA Staff
feedback.conditions: Not stated. Pre-2020 test, included because no newer KTM-family clutch test was found.
feedback.observed: Engages more quickly, hooks up better and is easier to modulate; helps most on starts. MXA calls it incremental, not a game-changer, and it adds no top speed. Cush bumpers are expected to last about five times longer than stock but still need replacement.
feedback.measured: Hub/plate $499.99; clutch pack $199.99; cover $169.95; main-shaft nut 59 ft-lb; stock Belleville 280 N/m

feedback.brand: various (JBI DIY kit, Race Tech spring conversion + Gold Valves, Dialed lugs with KYB SSS, WP 6500)
feedback.product: AER air-to-coil conversions (forum comparison)
feedback.author: OwenJakes, ParkingLotWheelies, AMetts, mark_swart, GoggleFiend904, AssangeMX and others
feedback.conditions: Individual owners; rider sizes vary (for example 6'4" and 220-230 lb)
feedback.observed: Individual experiences, not tests. JBI DIY on a GasGas (OwenJakes): a big improvement over stock but too harsh, losing top-of-stroke support in flat corners and small bumps. Race Tech spring plus Gold Valves (ParkingLotWheelies): better on chop, more bottoming resistance, sharper turning. AMetts (2021 FX350): a spring alone isn't worth about $600, but it is good with Gold Valves. mark_swart: a year on a Race Tech single-side setup and never happy; switched to Dialed lugs with YZ250F internals. GoggleFiend904 (2023 350 SX-F): Dialed adapters with 2022 SSS cartridges beat a cone valve, WP 6500 and a DIY AER kit, at about $500-600 net. AssangeMX: the stock air fork is stiffer and less comfortable than the 6500 but lighter and easier to wheelie over bumps. Luxon MX (a vendor) says single-sided forks create a left-right imbalance that can bind.
feedback.measured: Costs reported by users: Race Tech spring about $600; Dialed-type $500-900; used 6500 cartridges under $1,000

feedback.product: Single-spring AER conversion (with rear bladder)
feedback.author: scootscheerer, CR23, motoxracer723, Schlava, crc245, neysbo
feedback.conditions: Individual owners
feedback.observed: Individual experiences. CR23 (2019 350): noticeably better than a revalved air fork with a midvalve; estimates about 75% of the dual-spring benefit for half the price. motoxracer723 (2019 350 SX-F, then 2022 FC350): perhaps better than a revalved AER but not overwhelmingly, often felt asymmetric, and cost close to a KYB conversion. crc245 and neysbo prefer dual-spring conversions; Schlava says matched valving matters more than spring count. scootscheerer (2025 TC 300, 280 lb) bought a kit with a rear bladder for $2,080.
feedback.measured: $2,080 with rear bladder (one user)

feedback.brand: various (270mm floating/solid rotors, Tusk kit, MotoStuff)
feedback.product: Oversize front rotor (270mm)
feedback.author: AJ565, FGR01, Cobbler, Ob917
feedback.conditions: Individual owners
feedback.observed: Individual experiences. The consistent pattern is that the gain is a wider modulation window more than raw power. The stock brake locked up in wet, soft or sandy corners at lean, and the 270s did not (AJ565, FGR01). Helps when arm-pumped. Cobbler paired a Tusk kit with aggressive CM46 pads and needed little finger effort. No negatives reported.

feedback.brand: Ride Engineering / Luxon MX / FCP Racing
feedback.product: RE 23.5mm clamps; Luxon 23.5mm clamps; FCP engine mounts
feedback.author: Mr. Plump, dansfx, ithinkitsbroke, JK BRO
feedback.conditions: Individual owners
feedback.observed: Individual experiences. Mr. Plump (2024 350 SX-F): FCP mounts back to back felt plusher with better lean traction; he felt the RE 23.5 clamps helped the first two parts of a corner but had no data. feedback.measured: Mr. Plump reported a 2-second average lap improvement over 16 laps with the FCP mounts (self-reported)
